searchText: hey, we published part 2 of the repricing blog post series: https://zkevm.ethereum.foundation/blog/repricings-for-block-proving-part-2 <marcinbugaj> <@427491045308235776> , in hackmd you asked for an example of production code that is not UB and that leads to unaligned accesses. Here is a "kind of" instance of that: The Linux kernel uses unaligned accesses deliberately for speed, especially in data-processing paths. It provides safe accessors which emit code leading to unaligned accesses (get_unaligned, put_unaligned) and conditionally enables fast paths when the CPU supports it efficiently (CONFIG_HAVE_EFFICIENT_UNALIGNED_ACCESS). Examples (among many in the kernel): - https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/24d479d26b25bce5faea3ddd9fa8f3a6c3129ea7/include/crypto/utils.h#L18 - https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/24d479d26b25bce5faea3ddd9fa8f3a6c3129ea7/lib/lzo/lzo1x_compress.c#L66 That code leverages the fact that some architectures (x86_64, aarch64, some RV64 platforms) support unaligned accesses. The provided links show C code that leads to unaligned accesses (despite the fact that language spec calls it UB). <marcinbugaj> BTW Here is an unsolved Rust bug for RISCV64 that leads to unaligned accesses: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/145769 <justindrake> re: **@marcinbugaj** > BTW Here is an unsolved Rust bug for RISCV64 that leads to unaligned accesses: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/145769 When do you think we'll have a flavour of RISC-V as a Rust tier 1? <marcinbugaj> On the performance implications of not supporting unaligned accesses. https://rust.godbolt.org/z/6W7GcGvbd/ shows u64 deserialization from unaligned buffer (common in deserialization frameworks). A simple function that deserializes a u64 from a byte slice of unknown alignment explodes into many instructions (loads, shifts, ORs) when targeting a strict architecture. In contrast, on aarch64 https://rust.godbolt.org/z/8r4fxGTPr (which handles unaligned accesses), it often compiles to just one or two efficient load instructions. This directly impacts parsing performance and will impact EVM emulation. Interesting publication on unaligned accesses and performance: "Misaligned memory loads penalties in RISC-V Microcontrollers": https://reddi.unlam.edu.ar/index.php/ReDDi/article/download/177/332?inline=1 . That raises an important question what would be the cost of supporting unaligned accesses in zkVMs. <marcinbugaj> re: **@justindrake** > When do you think we'll have a flavour of RISC-V as a Rust tier 1? I think it's hard to tell unless the EF can devote some resources to work on Rust compiler for the desired platform. <alexanderlhicks> Yeah I wouldn't count on this in the short term, let alone having the target we are standardizing on (however that evolves) be the one that is made tier 1. I do think we can at least get a target we actually use to be tier 2 though. Beyond that is also depends on risc-v adoption more broadly (which is progressing...). <justindrake> re: **@marcinbugaj** > I think it's hard to tell unless the EF can devote some resources to work on Rust compiler for the desired platform. Can you quantify this (e.g. in dollars or man hours)? Just to clarify, my main point is that we should be intentional as of why we want this, not that we shouldn't do it I don't think the linux code is a counter-example because from what I can see, the get_unaligned method may or may not emit unaligned loads, see: ``` #define __get_unaligned_t(type, ptr) ({ \ const struct { type x; } __packed * __pptr = (typeof(__pptr))(ptr); \ __pptr->x; \ }) ``` I think this falls into the same bucket as `memcpy` where the alignment is set to 1 and its on the compiler to decide whether it does it via byte-by-byte or via an unaligned load +1 on performance, <@381789485777682434> for reference here; is there a significant/any performance degradation for air bender if the circuit only does aligned loads? For the emitted code you linked, the compiler may or may not emit an unaligned load, even if the hardware says it is supported The document for reference is https://hackmd.io/@kevaundray/SkUPg3LBWe I'm still unsure about the golang section. Was waiting for golang devs to explicitly modify the specs re unaligned loads, since it is ambiguous and confusing imo. PR for that is here: https://github.com/golang/go/pull/77215 <marcinbugaj> re: **@L1zkevm_bot** > <kevaundray> I don't think the linux code is a counter-example because from what I can see, the get_unaligned method may or may not emit unaligned loads, see: ``` #define __get_unaligned_t(type, ptr) ({ \ const struct { type x; } __packed * __pptr = (typeof(__pptr))(ptr); \ __pptr->x; \ }) ``` It was done with direct casting in older kernels. Here's an example: https://github.com/spotify/linux/blob/master/include/linux/unaligned/access_ok.h . Now indeed, they got rid of hardware specific stuff for unaligned accesses. Still, `get_unaligned()` function gets compiled in a way that "big" loads are emitted for unaligned addresses. For emitting big unaligned loads — this is only if the compiler wants to no? ie the code above does not force the compiler to emit unaligned loads similar to memcpy <marcinbugaj> re: **@L1zkevm_bot** > <kevaundray> For emitting big unaligned loads — this is only if the compiler wants to no? ie the code above does not force the compiler to emit unaligned loads similar to memcpy The code above forces compiler to emit unaligned loads. Casting in C and C++ enables that although it’s technically UB. That approach was used in the past in the Linux kernel To clarify, get_unaligned would force an unaligned load? Seems like it’s using __packed which says there is an alignment of 1? <marcinbugaj> The one with packed leaves the decision to the compiler. I was talking about the approach in older kernels which indeed forces unaligned accesses Ah right, I think if it's using UB to force the unaligned access, I would consider that a user bug irrespective of zk. ----------- The main overarching point that I'm validating is that ultimately, it is the compiler that decides whether an unaligned access is emitted in non-UB code. If code uses UB, then I think this would be a bug. For bare metal RISC-V, we can check but I think the compiler would not emit an unaligned load (in non-UB code) since that _could_ crash the device if unaligned access is not supported and there is no OS like linux to catch the trap and fix it up in software. So then imo the justification for adding unaligned access would be to guard against compiler bugs (that you noted have happened before) that hurt performance but do not affect correctness because everything else is a bug. This is assuming it is UB in Golang (still waiting for them to review the spec PR)

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<marcinbugaj> <@427491045308235776> , in hackmd you asked for an example of production code that is not UB and that leads to unaligned accesses. Here is a "kind of" instance of that:

The Linux kernel uses unaligned accesses deliberately for speed, especially in data-processing paths. It provides safe accessors which emit code leading to unaligned accesses (get_unaligned, put_unaligned) and conditionally enables fast paths when the CPU supports it efficiently (CONFIG_HAVE_EFFICIENT_UNALIGNED_ACCESS). Examples (among many in the kernel):
- https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/24d479d26b25bce5faea3ddd9fa8f3a6c3129ea7/include/crypto/utils.h#L18
- https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/24d479d26b25bce5faea3ddd9fa8f3a6c3129ea7/lib/lzo/lzo1x_compress.c#L66

That code leverages the fact that some architectures (x86_64, aarch64, some RV64 platforms) support unaligned accesses. The provided links show C code that leads to unaligned accesses (despite the fact that language spec calls it UB).

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<marcinbugaj> On the performance implications of not supporting unaligned accesses.

https://rust.godbolt.org/z/6W7GcGvbd/ shows u64 deserialization from unaligned buffer (common in deserialization frameworks). A simple function that deserializes a u64 from a byte slice of unknown alignment explodes into many instructions (loads, shifts, ORs) when targeting a strict architecture. In contrast, on aarch64 https://rust.godbolt.org/z/8r4fxGTPr (which handles unaligned accesses), it often compiles to just one or two efficient load instructions. This directly impacts parsing performance and will impact EVM emulation.

Interesting publication on unaligned accesses and performance: "Misaligned memory loads penalties in RISC-V Microcontrollers": https://reddi.unlam.edu.ar/index.php/ReDDi/article/download/177/332?inline=1 . That raises an important question what would be the cost of supporting unaligned accesses in zkVMs.

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
I don't think the linux code is a counter-example because from what I can see, the get_unaligned method may or may not emit unaligned loads, see:

```
#define __get_unaligned_t(type, ptr) ({                         \
    const struct { type x; } __packed * __pptr = (typeof(__pptr))(ptr); \
    __pptr->x;                                                  \
})
```

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content: I think this falls into the same bucket as `memcpy` where the alignment is set to 1 and its on the compiler to decide whether it does it via byte-by-byte or via an unaligned load

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
+1 on performance, <@381789485777682434> for reference here; is there a significant/any performance degradation for air bender if the circuit only does aligned loads?

For the emitted code you linked, the compiler may or may not emit an unaligned load, even if the hardware says it is supported

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<marcinbugaj> re: **@L1zkevm_bot**
> <kevaundray> I don't think the linux code is a counter-example because from what I can see, the get_unaligned method may or may not emit unaligned loads, see:

```
#define __get_unaligned_t(type, ptr) ({                         \
    const struct { type x; } __packed * __pptr = (typeof(__pptr))(ptr); \
    __pptr->x;                                                  \
})
```
It was done with direct casting in older kernels. Here's an example: https://github.com/spotify/linux/blob/master/include/linux/unaligned/access_ok.h . Now indeed, they got rid of hardware specific stuff for unaligned accesses. Still, `get_unaligned()` function gets compiled in a way that "big" loads are emitted for unaligned addresses.

excerpts.author: kevaundray
excerpts.content:
Ah right, I think if it's using UB to force the unaligned access, I would consider that a user bug irrespective of zk.

-----------

The main overarching point that I'm validating is that ultimately, it is the compiler that decides whether an unaligned access is emitted in non-UB code. If code uses UB, then I think this would be a bug.

For bare metal RISC-V, we can check but I think the compiler would not emit an unaligned load (in non-UB code) since that _could_ crash the device if unaligned access is not supported and there is no OS like linux to catch the trap and fix it up in software.

So then imo the justification for adding unaligned access would be to guard against compiler bugs (that you noted have happened before) that hurt performance but do not affect correctness because everything else is a bug.

This is assuming it is UB in Golang (still waiting for them to review the spec PR)
